analysis_trace: Trial NCT06590532 is a French multi-center RCT evaluating Cydar-EV automated image fusion system versus standard fluoroscopy for endovascular aortic aneurysm repair (EVAR) and aorto-iliac revascularization. Primary endpoint is cost-consequence analysis; secondary endpoints include radiation dose, contrast dose, technical/clinical success, mortality, and quality of life.
Evidence retrieved: ARIA trial protocol publications (2024) confirm this is the same trial evaluating clinical, technical, and cost-effectiveness. No outcome results available as of knowledge cutoff.

Image fusion technology mechanism: Cydar-EV uses AI-driven computer vision to fuse pre-procedural CT with intra-operative fluoroscopy, potentially reducing fluoroscopy time, radiation exposure, and contrast volume compared to standard roadmap imaging.

Indirect evidence from similar fusion technologies in EVAR suggests radiation dose reduction of 30-50% and contrast reduction of 20-40% is biologically plausible based on improved visualization reducing need for repeated angiographic runs.
Technical success in standard EVAR typically exceeds 95%; image fusion may improve precision but effect on technical success rate likely modest given already high baseline.
30-day mortality for elective EVAR is typically 1-3% in contemporary series; image fusion guidance unlikely to significantly alter this established safety profile.

Cost-effectiveness prediction depends on incremental cost of fusion system versus savings from reduced procedure time, complications, and resource utilization. French healthcare perspective analysis with 18-month horizon.
Evidence gaps: No published outcome data from this specific trial; no direct numeric evidence for Cydar-EV effect sizes; cost data not publicly available; long-term clinical outcomes uncertain.

Evidence role assignments: Protocol documents provide design confirmation (indirect_direction); similar fusion technologies provide mechanism support and directional estimates (mechanism_background); no direct numeric evidence available for precise effect size estimation.

analysis_trace: Trial NCT06590532 is a French multi-center RCT evaluating Cydar-EV automated image fusion system versus standard fluoroscopy for endovascular aortic aneurysm repair (EVAR) and aorto-iliac revascularization. Primary endpoint is cost-consequence analysis; secondary endpoints include radiation dose, contrast dose, technical/clinical success, mortality, and quality of life.
Evidence retrieved: ARIA trial protocol publications (2024) confirm this is the same trial evaluating clinical, technical, and cost-effectiveness. No outcome results available as of knowledge cutoff.

Image fusion technology mechanism: Cydar-EV uses AI-driven computer vision to fuse pre-procedural CT with intra-operative fluoroscopy, potentially reducing fluoroscopy time, radiation exposure, and contrast volume compared to standard roadmap imaging.

Indirect evidence from similar fusion technologies in EVAR suggests radiation dose reduction of 30-50% and contrast reduction of 20-40% is biologically plausible based on improved visualization reducing need for repeated angiographic runs.
Technical success in standard EVAR typically exceeds 95%; image fusion may improve precision but effect on technical success rate likely modest given already high baseline.
30-day mortality for elective EVAR is typically 1-3% in contemporary series; image fusion guidance unlikely to significantly alter this established safety profile.

Cost-effectiveness prediction depends on incremental cost of fusion system versus savings from reduced procedure time, complications, and resource utilization. French healthcare perspective analysis with 18-month horizon.
Evidence gaps: No published outcome data from this specific trial; no direct numeric evidence for Cydar-EV effect sizes; cost data not publicly available; long-term clinical outcomes uncertain.

Evidence role assignments: Protocol documents provide design confirmation (indirect_direction); similar fusion technologies provide mechanism support and directional estimates (mechanism_background); no direct numeric evidence available for precise effect size estimation.

analysis_trace: Trial NCT06590532 is a French RCT evaluating Cydar-EV automated image fusion vs standard X-ray fluoroscopy for EVAR/aorto-iliac procedures. Primary endpoint is cost consequence analysis; secondary endpoints include radiation dose, contrast dose, ITU/HDU stay, technical/clinical success, 30-day mortality, QoL, and cost-effectiveness.

Evidence retrieved: ARIA trial protocol (ISRCTN13832085) and statistical analysis plan (PMC12042510) describe the UK sister trial using same Cydar-EV technology. King's College London reports (2022) cite mean 35% reduction in fluoroscopy time, 41% reduction in contrast, 1-hour reduction in operating time with Cydar-EV.

Meta-analysis evidence (SAGE JEVT 2020) shows image fusion significantly reduces contrast volume, fluoroscopy time, and procedure time in complex EVAR; reduces contrast and procedure time in standard EVAR. Radiation dose reduction suggested but not consistently significant across all studies.

Evidence role assessment: ARIA protocol and KCL reports provide indirect_direction for Cydar-EV benefits on radiation/contrast/procedure time. Meta-analysis provides indirect_direction for fusion imaging benefits. No direct results from NCT06590532 available before cutoff.

Population match: ARIA trial (UK) and NCT06590532 (France) both use Cydar-EV for EVAR with similar inclusion criteria (elective AAA, trained surgeons). Evidence_role: indirect_direction with good generalizability.

Primary endpoint (cost consequence): No direct cost data available. Based on ARIA trial design and reported efficiency gains (shorter procedure time, reduced complications), fusion guidance likely cost-effective but exact magnitude uncertain. Predicted direction: favorable to fusion group.
Secondary-0 (X-ray dose): Evidence supports reduction. Predicted mean reduction 25-40% vs control based on prior Cydar studies. Confidence moderate.
Secondary-1 (physician X-ray dose): Operator exposure parallels patient dose reduction. Predicted mean reduction 25-35%.
Secondary-2 (contrast dose): Strong evidence for reduction. Meta-analysis and KCL data support ~40% reduction. Confidence higher.
Secondary-3 (ITU/HDU stay): No direct evidence. Elective EVAR typically has low ITU admission. Predicted no significant difference between groups.
Secondary-4 (technical success): Fusion improves visualization and positioning. Predicted higher technical success in fusion group, but both groups expected high success (>95%).
Secondary-5 (clinical success): 1-month patency/exclusion expected high in both groups. Fusion may have slight advantage due to better positioning.
Secondary-6 (30-day mortality): Elective EVAR mortality typically 1-2%. No expected difference between groups.
Secondary-7 (QoL): EQ-5D-5L at 30 days. No expected difference; both groups minimally invasive.
Secondary-8 (5-year cost-effectiveness): Long-term projection; based on efficiency gains and reduced reinterventions, likely favorable to fusion but highly uncertain.
Key uncertainties: No direct French trial results; cost data not available; long-term outcomes speculative; trial still recruiting at cutoff.

你是一名临床试验终点预测与循证医学分析专家。

你的任务是：基于知识截止日期之前公开可获得的证据，预测临床试验指定终点的结果。

规则：
1. 这是预测任务，不是结果检索任务。
2. 即使直接证据不足，也必须尽力给出预测。
3. 证据不足时，应降低 confidence，并明确说明不确定性，但不能仅因为证据不足而拒绝预测。
4. 只有在终点定义缺失、终点无法识别或预测目标无法映射时，才使用 not_evaluable。
5. 不得使用知识截止日期之后公开的信息。
6. 不得把试验状态、论文发表、药物批准或模型评分直接视为终点成功证据。
7. 每个 endpoint_id 必须单独预测。
8. 每个治疗组、时间点和统计目标必须单独保留。
9. 不要输出隐藏思维链或内部逐步推理过程。
10. 但必须输出完整、可公开审计的证据分析，包括证据来源、证据类型、证据与预测之间的联系以及主要不确定性。
11. 引用必须是真实使用过的公开来源 URL；没有真实 URL 时，不要声称有引用。
12. 如果无法确认某个数值，应给出基于证据的预测值，并在 uncertainty 和 rationale 中说明不确定性；不要凭空声称已经观察到该结果。
13. 证据来源必须可追溯：只有当前会话工具成功返回的公开记录、正文片段和 URL 才能称为“已检索证据”。工具返回 returned=0、source_unavailable 或空 results 时，不得把该来源当作证据。

PMC Copyright notice PMCID: PMC10962083 PMID: 38528619 Abstract Background Endovascular repair of aortic aneurysmal disease is established due to perceived advantages in patient survival, reduced postoperative complications, and shorter hospital lengths of stay. High spatial and contrast resolution 3D CT angiography images are used to plan the procedures and inform device selection and manufacture, but in standard care, the surgery is performed using image-guidance from 2D X-ray fluoroscopy with injection of nephrotoxic contrast material to visualise the blood vessels. This study aims to assess the benefit to patients, practitioners, and the health service of a novel image fusion medical device (Cydar EV), which allows this high-resolution 3D information to be available to operators at the time of surgery. Methods The trial is a multi-centre, open label, two-armed randomised controlled clinical trial of 340 patient, randomised 1:1 to either standard treatment in endovascular aneurysm repair or treatment using Cydar EV, a CE-marked medical device comprising of cloud computing, augmented intelligence, and computer vision. The primary outcome is procedural time, with secondary outcomes of procedural efficiency, technical effectiveness, patient outcomes, and cost-effectiveness. Patients with a clinical diagnosis of AAA or TAAA suitable for endovascular repair and able to provide written informed consent will be invited to participate. Discussion This trial is the first randomised controlled trial evaluating advanced image fusion technology in endovascular aortic surgery and is well placed to evaluate the effect of this technology on patient outcomes and cost to the NHS. The image guidance system minimises exposure to radiation and kidney-toxic contrast and shortens the duration of surgery. The demonstrated success of the technology led to the development of the spinout Cydar Medical in 2012. The technology fills a clinical gap created by endovascular aortic repair (EVAR), a type of surgery performed inside your aorta using long, thin tubes called catheters to place a stent surrounded with a fabric liner, together called a stent graft, to reinforce the weak spots in the wall. Cydar EV is a digital technology using cloud-computing, big-data and artificial intelligence which has the potential to improve the predictability of individual outcomes and the consistency of outcomes of image-guided procedures in the NHS. Dr Rachel Clough, Clinical Senior Lecturer, Department of Biomedical Engineering at the School of Biomedical Engineering & Imaging Sciences While EVAR is an example of how minimally invasive procedures are revolutionizing the management of cardiovascular disease, there are numerous technical and procedural challenges, including a loss of spatial information during positioning of the device, requiring the surgeon to try to visualise the 3D anatomy using a 2D screen. Imprecise visualisation of the anatomy and positioning of the device leads to high rates of re-intervention and complications, requiring further patient hospital admissions. The lack of 3D visualisation also slows down the procedure and leads to an increase in the amount of ionising radiation and concern of the volume of kidney toxic contrast agent (used to delineate the blood vessels). Cydar-EV ensures a significant reduction in the amount of x-rays used, with researchers citing a mean 35 percent reduction in x-ray fluoroscopy screening time, 41 percent reduction in the amount of iodinated kidney toxic contrast, a one-hour reduction in the average operating time. There was also a significant reduction in exposure to radiation for operators. The technology results in reduced patient exposure to anaesthesia and ionising radiation, lowering surgical site infection and reducing adverse events. Surgeons now have real-time, fully integrated 3D visualisation through the EVAR procedure with much greater spatial information than was achieved by previous technology. Cydar technology will lead to more precise device positioning and enhance procedural success. While there are a number of AI companies in the diagnostic imaging space, Cydar is currently the only company in the world with a CE marked, FDA-cleared product using cloud and AI technology to inform and influence surgery in real-time. There are traditional imaging companies that use hardware to achieve less accurate and reliable image fusion but these are not considered competitors as they do not aggregate data and therefore cannot develop the same intelligent insights and channel for new products. PMC Copyright notice PMCID: PMC12042510 PMID: 40307841 Abstract Background Aortic aneurysms, a significant cause of mortality, particularly in individuals aged 55 years and older, have witnessed a transformative shift in treatment strategies with the advent of endovascular surgery. Cydar-EV is an innovative image fusion technology that can augment preoperative planning and surgical guidance of endovascular aneurysm repair (EVAR). The ARIA trial aims to evaluate the efficacy of using Cydar-EV with EVAR procedures to reduce operating time while enhancing procedural precision, patient outcomes, and cost-effectiveness. This paper describes the statistical analysis plan for the study. Methods/design The ARIA trial, a phase III, multi-centre, open-label, two-armed, parallel groups randomised controlled surgical trial, seeks to recruit 340 patients diagnosed with abdominal or thoraco-abdominal aortic aneurysms. Participants are randomly assigned to receive either standard endovascular repair or an endovascular repair assisted by Cydar-EV for planning and surgical guidance. Primary and secondary outcomes are assessed at baseline, 4–12 weeks, and 52 weeks. The primary outcome measure is procedure duration at baseline, while additional secondary outcomes are recorded at various time points and include indicators for technical effectiveness, patient outcomes, procedure efficiency, and cost-effectiveness. We plan to analyse the patient outcome data according to the treatment they received regardless of initial allocation. The statistical analysis plan outlines methods for handling missing data, covariates for adjusted analyses, and planned sensitivity analyses to ensure robust evaluation of treatment effects. Trial registration The trial was registered with the ISRCTN register on 03/12/2021, number ISRCTN13832085. Background Aortic aneurysm, the second most prevalent condition affecting the aorta after atherosclerosis, stands as the fifteenth leading cause of death among individuals aged 55 years and older and nineteenth overall. The advent of endovascular surgery marks a significant shift towards minimally invasive procedures. Endovascular aneurysm repair (EVAR) has rapidly gained precedence over open aortic surgery, driven by perceived advantages in patient survival, reduced postoperative complications, and shorter hospital stays [ 1 ]. The pre-operative planning of EVAR surgery involves the use of computed tomography (CT) scans to reconstruct 3D images for assessing access and determining the optimal type, configuration, and sizing of the implantable medical device. During surgery, a 2D X-ray fluoroscopy, coupled with the injection of nephrotoxic contrast material, is employed to visualise blood vessels and guide the procedure. However, device positioning errors may still occur resulting in variability in patient outcomes which in many cases necessitates secondary interventions [ 2 ]. In addition, imprecise positioning can lead to serious and even fatal complications raising concerns about cost-effectiveness [ 3 , 4 ]. Previous solutions to enhance visualisation during EVAR have included manually aligned, operating table-tracked 3D-2D image overlay. This technology, available in from GE, Siemens, and Philips, can be deemed too costly as it necessitates design, installation, and maintenance of a hybrid operating room. A survey across 10 US centres revealed that although equipped with 3D overlay capabilities, clinicians refrained from its use due to disruptions in clinical workflow and clinically significant image positioning errors [ 5 ]. In contrast, Cydar-EV image fusion, a CE-marked medical device, employs computer vision to automatically and in real-time fuse pre-procedural 3D images with intra-operative 2D fluoroscopy. Unlike other methods, Cydar-EV provides surgeons with real-time fully integrated 3D visualisation throughout the EVAR procedure. The computer vision, a form of artificial intelligence utilising NHS digital-approved, GDPR-compliant high-performance cloud computing, relies solely on existing patient data without introducing new imaging. Importantly, it seamlessly integrates into existing clinical workflows, requires no user interaction, involves no additional ionising radiation or iodinated contrast, and is compatible with both fixed and mobile X-ray systems. The ‘ARIA’ (ARtificially Intelligent image fusion system versus standard treatment to guide endovascular Aortic aneurysm repair) trial is a multi-centre randomised controlled trial designed to compare the operation time of patients undergoing EVAR. The study aims to determine whether the implementation of Cydar-EV during EVAR offers superiority over the current standard procedure, without Cydar-EV, in terms of achieving a shorter operation time, reduced costs, and enhanced procedural efficiency, while maintaining equally effective technical outcomes and positive patient results. Here we outline the statistical analysis plan intended for generating the main results of the ARIA trial. This plan has been finalised while the data collection is still ongoing. Study design The ARIA trial protocol has been published previously [ 6 ]. In brief, ARIA is a multi-centre, open label, two-armed, parallel groups randomised controlled surgical trial comparing Cydar-EV to conventional surgical procedure. Patients are recruited from 10 sites across the UK. After obtaining written informed consent and confirming eligibility, participants undergoing endovascular aortic aneurysm repair are being randomly assigned to procedures with or without Cydar-EV for planning and surgical guidance. Randomisation method The randomisation, performed at the patient level, follows a 1:1 ratio and utilises minimisation methods. The King’s Clinical Trials Unit (KCTU) at King’s College London manages the randomisation process through a web-based bespoke randomisation system. analysis_trace: Trial NCT06590532 is a French RCT evaluating Cydar-EV automated image fusion vs standard X-ray fluoroscopy for EVAR/aorto-iliac procedures. Primary endpoint is cost consequence analysis; secondary endpoints include radiation dose, contrast dose, ITU/HDU stay, technical/clinical success, 30-day mortality, QoL, and cost-effectiveness.

Evidence retrieved: ARIA trial protocol (ISRCTN13832085) and statistical analysis plan (PMC12042510) describe the UK sister trial using same Cydar-EV technology. King's College London reports (2022) cite mean 35% reduction in fluoroscopy time, 41% reduction in contrast, 1-hour reduction in operating time with Cydar-EV.

Meta-analysis evidence (SAGE JEVT 2020) shows image fusion significantly reduces contrast volume, fluoroscopy time, and procedure time in complex EVAR; reduces contrast and procedure time in standard EVAR. Radiation dose reduction suggested but not consistently significant across all studies.

Evidence role assessment: ARIA protocol and KCL reports provide indirect_direction for Cydar-EV benefits on radiation/contrast/procedure time. Meta-analysis provides indirect_direction for fusion imaging benefits. No direct results from NCT06590532 available before cutoff.

Population match: ARIA trial (UK) and NCT06590532 (France) both use Cydar-EV for EVAR with similar inclusion criteria (elective AAA, trained surgeons). Evidence_role: indirect_direction with good generalizability.

Primary endpoint (cost consequence): No direct cost data available. Based on ARIA trial design and reported efficiency gains (shorter procedure time, reduced complications), fusion guidance likely cost-effective but exact magnitude uncertain. Predicted direction: favorable to fusion group.
Secondary-0 (X-ray dose): Evidence supports reduction. Predicted mean reduction 25-40% vs control based on prior Cydar studies. Confidence moderate.
Secondary-1 (physician X-ray dose): Operator exposure parallels patient dose reduction. Predicted mean reduction 25-35%.
Secondary-2 (contrast dose): Strong evidence for reduction. Meta-analysis and KCL data support ~40% reduction. Confidence higher.
Secondary-3 (ITU/HDU stay): No direct evidence. Elective EVAR typically has low ITU admission. Predicted no significant difference between groups.
Secondary-4 (technical success): Fusion improves visualization and positioning. Predicted higher technical success in fusion group, but both groups expected high success (>95%).
Secondary-5 (clinical success): 1-month patency/exclusion expected high in both groups. Fusion may have slight advantage due to better positioning.
Secondary-6 (30-day mortality): Elective EVAR mortality typically 1-2%. No expected difference between groups.
Secondary-7 (QoL): EQ-5D-5L at 30 days. No expected difference; both groups minimally invasive.
Secondary-8 (5-year cost-effectiveness): Long-term projection; based on efficiency gains and reduced reinterventions, likely favorable to fusion but highly uncertain.
Key uncertainties: No direct French trial results; cost data not available; long-term outcomes speculative; trial still recruiting at cutoff.
